vignette:
Margaret Doyle is a 70-year-old widowed woman of European American background who has spent most of her adult life working in hospitality and now manages a mid-sized hotel. She described the traumatic event as something that still feels both far away in time and completely present in her body. It happened on an evening when she was leaving work after handling a difficult disturbance involving guests in the lobby. Police had been called to the property. Margaret had expected that, as the hotel manager, she would help clarify what had happened and then return to the routine of closing out the day. Instead, in the confusion of a crowded entrance, raised voices, and officers moving quickly, she was handled with force by police. In telling it, she remembers the density of people in the lobby and on the sidewalk, the pressure of bodies close together, the sense that no one was listening as she tried to explain who she was and that she worked there. What has stayed with her is not only the physical aggression but the shock of being treated as if her words did not matter while others watched.

In the days after, Margaret found that the event returned to her in sharp, unwanted thoughts. She did not have to be trying to remember it. She could be reviewing staffing schedules in her office or walking through the breakfast area before the morning rush, and something in her surroundings would abruptly pull the entire scene back with startling completeness. A cluster of guests gathering too closely near the front desk, the swell of voices in the lobby during check-in, or simply the feel of navigating through a crowded elevator bank could bring back the full memory without warning. When that happened, the recollection was not vague or distant. She said the memories were painfully clear and detailed, as if she could again see exactly where everyone was standing and hear the tone of the officers' voices. Most upsetting was that remembering it did not feel like ordinary remembering; the same terror came back with it, immediate enough that she felt as though she were there again.

Over the following months, she began reorganizing her days around the possibility of being caught off guard. At work, she started timing her movements to avoid the busiest stretches in the lobby. She delegated more face-to-face guest issues to junior staff and remained in the back office when tour groups arrived. As hotel manager, she had once taken pride in being visible, steady, and available on the floor. Now she found herself watching the crowding near the entrance and calculating alternate routes through service corridors. This had practical consequences. Staff noticed that Margaret was less present during peak check-in times, and she was distressed by how unlike herself this felt. She had been known for calm competence in hectic environments, and it unsettled her that she no longer trusted herself to stand in the middle of them.

The anniversary of the event became especially difficult. As the date approached, the unwanted thoughts became more frequent, and on the day itself she found the memory nearly impossible to hold at a distance. She described feeling pulled back into the event by the calendar alone, dreading the day well in advance and then moving through it with a sense of impending terror. Even when she tried to keep busy with work, she remained acutely aware of what date it was and what had happened on that same day the year before.

Margaret speaks with particular bitterness about the meaning the event took on for her. She had always believed that if something went wrong, the police and other public institutions were the people who were supposed to restore order and keep people safe. Since the incident, she has come to believe that the people and systems that should have protected her failed her instead. She returns to this not as an abstract opinion but as a personal rupture: she was a professional trying to do her job, in her own workplace, and the very authority she expected to rely on became the source of danger. Alongside that is a painful alteration in how she sees herself. Widowed for years, Margaret had built a strong sense of identity around being capable, composed, and resilient. Now she says she does not know herself anymore. What frightens her most is the conviction that she has changed permanently for the worse, that whatever was solid in her before the incident has been damaged beyond repair.

By the time she sought help, the strain of living this way had become harder to conceal. The combination of sudden, vivid recollections in the hotel environment, dread surrounding crowded spaces, and the annual return of the date itself had narrowed her world. She came to treatment not because the memory had faded, but because it had not. She wants some way to live in her workplace and in her own mind without being overtaken so suddenly. At the same time, she is afraid that seeking help may confirm what she already suspects-that the person she was before that night is gone for good.
